3.  26-54987  Recommendation to review and discuss the FY 2026 Continuum of Care (CoC)
  Scoring and Ranking Policy.

  • Health Department staff Joseph Botelho provided an update on the 2026
  Scoring and Ranking Policies.
  • HUD requires CoCs to review, asses and score project applications for
  performance as part of the CoC program competition.
  • High level updates were discussed. We naturally weigh permanent
  supportive housing and rapid rehousing, higher than traditional housing and
  supportive services.
  • Performance scores are used to rank all projects for funding consideration,
  scores being used to rank projects, scores are also used to determine
  reallocation for grants demonstrating poor performance, in alignment with the
  Long Beach CoC reallocation policy.
  • Staff went over the metric review for project performance, fiscal performance,
  HMIS and supportive service participation requirements.
  • A sliding scale scoring awards points proportionally within the threshold
  range instead of awarded only fixed-point values at the lower and upper
  thresholds. This helps reduce clustering at fixed point values, more
  accurately reflects actual performance, and strengthens the fairness and
  precision of project making.
  • Ranking by project type and threshold separates projects based on whether
  they meet a minimum performance threshold and then ranks projects by
  project type within each threshold group.
  • The Ad Hoc Scoring and Ranking workgroup will review the CoC Board
  feedback.
  • Board members have questions regarding the updates presented.

  A motion was made by Member Shuford, seconded by Member Martins, to

4.  26-54988  Recommendation to review and discuss the Long Beach Continuum of Care (CoC)
  Reallocation Policies and Procedures.

  • Health Department staff member Joseph Botelho provided an update on the
  Reallocation Policy and Procedure revisions. Reallocation is the process
  through which the CoC shifts funds, either in whole or in part, from existing
  renewed CoC-funded projects to create one or more new projects aimed at
  improving overall system performance. The two types of reallocation
  discussed were involuntary and voluntary reallocation.
  • The proposed reallocation policy would define the circumstances under
  which CoC funds may be shifted, reduced, or reallocated. Staff noted that
  performance improvement efforts would instead be addressed through
  separate technical assistance and monitoring guidance. Performance-based
  reallocation standards discussed included utilization and chronic
  underutilization.
  • The Ad Hoc Reallocation Workgroup will continue reviewing feedback
  provided by the CoC Board.
  • Board member Scott raised questions regarding agencies subject to
  reallocation and whether underspent projects could impact eligibility for
  future funding opportunities. Staff responded and provided clarification.
  • Board member Shufford also commented on the proposed reallocation
  thresholds.Staff responded once the competition is out the Board will have to
  meet again to go over the future changes based on the competition.
  • A member of the public provided public comment regarding the NOFO.

  A motion was made by Member Scott, seconded by Member Shuford, to
  approve recommendation. The motion carried by the following vote:

  Yes:  7  Boyce, Diles III, Martins, Tan, Scott, Shuford, Wee
  No:  0  None
  Recused: 0  None
  Abstain: 0  None
  Absent: 6  Amick, Brown-Shock, Lock, McFadzen, Rockenbach, Topolewski

  • Health Department staff Joseph Botelho provided a brief update.
  • HUD is expected to release the 2026 Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO)
  by June 1, with applications due August 26.Long Beach had 17 projects
  approved in the second-quarter CSC program renewal funding
  announcements; one project was not included but is expected to be awarded
  later
  • HUD plans to carry forward many elements of the 2025 NOFO, including:
  o At least 60% of Annual Renewal Demand (ARD) guaranteed in Tier 1
  funding.
  o Potential 30% cap on permanent housing funding.
  o Increased emphasis on unsheltered homelessness outcomes,
  transitional housing, outreach, law enforcement coordination, and
  supportive services.
  • Staff warned that a 30% cap on permanent housing could reduce local
  permanent housing funding by approximately $5.5 million, creating
  significant strategic and funding challenges.
  • The Ad Hoc Funding Priorities Workgroup will review the Boards feedback.

6.  26-54991  Recommendation to review the performance and close-out of the Community
  Development Block Grant–Coronavirus (CDBG-CV) funds utilized for the Project
  Homekey site located at 1725 Long Beach Boulevard.

  • Bureau Manager Paul Duncan provided an update eon the CDBG-CV Close-
  Out and Performance Review Project Homekey at 1725 Long Beach Blvd.
  funded through the CARES ACT through HUD. The state allocated $50
  million in May of 2021, the intended use was to prevent, prepare and
  respond to COVID-19.
  • The Homeless Services Bureau submitted an application to support
  conversion of the Project Homekey site into non-congregate interim housing,
  the goal is toi develop into permanent housing. The total project investment
  is $5,100,000 and expected to be complete by June 30,2025.
  • The project was originally planned for Permanent Supportive Housing and
  adapted to temporarily operate as a non-congregate Interim Housing, there
  are 99 units and a total of 323 participants served. The target population are

7.  26-54995  Recommendation to review and approve proposed budget reallocations
  and amendments to projects funded through the Long Beach Continuum of Care
  (CoC) Unified Funding Agency (UFA) Grant Agreement for Operating Dates July
  1, 2025, through June 30, 2026.

  • Health Department staff Joseph Botelho explained that the CoC, as a Unified
  Funding Agency, has authority to temporarily shift funds between projects
  during the operating year with board approval.
  • Staff proposed a one-time temporary reallocation of underspent project funds
  to avoid returning money to HUD before the June 30 deadline.
  • Projects with projected underspending above 25% of their annual budget
  were identified for possible recapture of 90% of unused projected balances.
  Agencies were given an opportunity to revise spending projections before
  final decisions.
  • Over the past five years, the CoC has returned approximately $3.3 million
  (8.29% of awarded funding) to HUD due to underspending. Staff stated this
  reflects insufficient portfolio and funding management.
  • The proposed temporary reallocation would move roughly $1.2–$1.3 million
  in projected unused funds into the Multi-Service Center (MSC) project to
  ensure the funding is spent before expiration.
  • Staff emphasized the reallocation is temporary and projects will regain their
  full budgets in the next grant term beginning July 1.
  • Agencies losing temporary funds are still required to maintain contracted
  service levels and participant outcomes.
  • Staff recommended implementing more active quarterly monitoring and
  oversight of project spending and performance moving forward.

  individuals losing Emergency Housing Voucher (EHV) assistance. Staff
  explained the funds are time-limited, making that use infeasible before the

  • The board approved the temporary reallocation proposal by roll call vote.
